title: Gauss-elimination (row-rank) method and consistency
summary: Gauss-elimination/row-rank procedure; echelon reduction and back-substitution; unique, infinite and inconsistent systems; homogeneous rank tests; parameter cases.
transcription_policy: Notebook meaning and class-work order are preserved, but physical notebook page breaks are treated as provenance only. Student-facing notes group each complete worked example into one accordion so an example is never split into 'beginning' and 'completion' sections. Visible notebook slips are corrected only in clearly labelled verification text; incomplete class work is completed by PankusDesk and labelled as such.

blocks.text: It is used to test whether a system is consistent and to solve it when it is consistent.
The unknowns are eliminated successively using row transformations until the augmented matrix is in echelon form. The unknowns are then obtained by back-substitution.

items.title: Example 1 — Solve by Gauss-elimination method
paragraphs: Form the augmented matrix and apply \(R_2\to R_2-2R_1\), \(R_3\to R_3-4R_1\):
Here \(\rho(A)=\rho(A|B)=3=n\), so the system has a unique solution.
Back-substitution gives \(-12z=-36\Rightarrow z=3\), then \(-y+2z=4\Rightarrow y=2\), and finally \(x+2y+z=8\Rightarrow x=1\).

items.title: Example 4 — Solve the homogeneous system
paragraphs: There are three pivots, so \(\rho(A)=3=n\). A homogeneous system with full rank has only the trivial solution.

math_mismatch.label: Class-note arithmetic slip
math_mismatch.message: The notebook displays \([0,-3,1]\) after \(R_2\to R_2-2R_1\). The correct row is \([0,-2,1]\). Continuing with the corrected row still gives rank 3, so the notebook's final conclusion is unchanged.

items.title: Example 5 — Find parameter values for unique, many, or no solutions
question_paragraphs: Find \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) so that the system has (i) a unique solution, (ii) many solutions, or (iii) no solution:
paragraphs: (i) For a unique solution, the third pivot must be non-zero: \(\lambda-5\ne0\). Hence \(\lambda\ne5\); \(\mu\) may be any real number.
(ii) For infinitely many solutions, the last row must become all zeros: \(\lambda=5\) and \(\mu=9\).
(iii) For no solution, the coefficient part of the last row must be zero while the augmented entry is non-zero: \(\lambda=5\), \(\mu\ne9\).
